extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and practitioners of poetics and drama (playwrights, critics)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for composing and staging tragedy: how to construct plot, effect recognitions, shape diction and thought, and handle chorus/acting so as to produce natural and convincing dramatic effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition by tokens/formal proof (less artistic)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognition effected by tokens or formal proofs (e.g., tokens, amulets) is regarded as a less artistic mode of recognition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: tokens used for the express purpose of proof are less artistic than recognitions arising from the incident itself. Such mechanical proofs are inferior because they do not arise naturally from the action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition invented by the poet (self-declaration)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognitions in which a character simply declares himself (the poet makes the character speak what the plot does not require) are wanting in art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Orestes in Iphigenia revealing himself by speaking — this is akin to the token-fault because the recognition is manufactured by the poet rather than emerging organically from the action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition by memory/association (sight or song awakens feeling)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognition can depend on memory when seeing or hearing an object awakens recollection and emotion, leading to recognition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: hero weeps on seeing a picture; Odysseus recognizes through a minstrel’s song. This kind is more natural than pure invention and can be effective when triggered plausibly by sensory cues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition by process of reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognition may be achieved by deliberate inference (reasoning from resemblance or circumstance).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: in the Choephori—‘Someone resembling me has come; no one resembles me but Orestes; therefore Orestes has come.’ This kind is legitimate when the reasoning is natural and probable within the situation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composite/false-inference recognitions (inferior)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognitions that rely on false inference or expectation (a character expects recognition that does not actually occur) are considered defective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: the disguised Odysseus expects another character to recognise the bow though that character has not seen it; creating recognition by manufactured expectation is false inference and inferior artistic practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best recognition: incident-derived/natural recognitions
rubrics_metrics.description: The best recognitions arise naturally from the incidents themselves — startling discoveries that follow plausibly from the action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Oedipus’ recognition and Iphigenia’s letter — recognitions that are natural to the situation dispense with artificial tokens and are superior artistically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visualisation of the scene (place the scene before the poet’s eyes)
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet should place the scene, as far as possible, before his eyes to see everything vividly and avoid inconsistencies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Working with the scene vividly in mind helps the poet discover what is in keeping with the action and prevents stage oversights (example: Carcinus failure where a stage oversight offended the audience).

rubrics_metrics.name: Work out play with appropriate gestures and delivery
rubrics_metrics.description: A play should be worked out with appropriate gestures and modes of delivery so that emotions register convincingly on stage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Actors who truly feel emotion produce more convincing performances: those agitated storm, those angry rage. Gesture and delivery belong to the art of staging and help produce life-like reality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sketch general outline then fill in episodes
rubrics_metrics.description: When composing the story, first sketch the general plan (overall outline) then fill in and amplify episodes and details.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Iphigenia — sketch the central situation (sacrifice, disappearance, transport, brother’s arrival) then supply episodes that are relevant to that plan; some elements (like oracle motives) may be outside the action proper.

rubrics_metrics.name: Episodes must be relevant to the action
rubrics_metrics.description: Episodes included in the drama should be relevant to and serve the action; avoid extraneous incidents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use episodes to develop the plot (e.g., Orestes’ madness and purificatory rite) but keep them short in drama form — irrelevant or lengthy episodes bloat the drama and approach epicness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragedy structure: Complication and Unravelling (Dénouement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every tragedy falls into two parts: the Complication (from beginning to turning-point) and the Unravelling (from the change to the end).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define the Complication as events leading to the turning-point; the Unravelling follows the change in fortune to conclusion. Use this partition to shape coherent dramatic action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kinds of tragedy (Complex, Pathetic, Ethical, Simple) and aim to combine merits
rubrics_metrics.description: There are four kinds of tragedy: the Complex (depends on reversal and recognition), the Pathetic (motive is passion), the Ethical (motive is ethical), and the Simple; poet should, if possible, combine the most important poetic merits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics expect excellence across multiple lines; where possible aim to include several merits rather than specialize narrowly in one branch.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid Epic structure and multiplicity of plots
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid treating a tragedy as an Epic structure (multiplicity of plots or dramatizing an entire epic tale).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select a portion of a large story rather than the whole (examples: dramatizing the whole Fall of Troy or the whole tale of Niobe results in failure or poor stage success). Tragedy requires focused selection and appropriate magnitude for each part.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot identity as test for sameness/difference
rubrics_metrics.description: A useful test for judging whether one tragedy is the same as another is whether their Complication and Unravelling are the same (plot identity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many poets tie the knot (Complication) well but unravel it ill; mastery of both knot-tying and unravelling is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chorus as an integral actor
rubrics_metrics.description: The Chorus should be regarded as one of the actors — an integral part that shares in the action rather than serving as irrelevant interludes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer the Sophoclean practice where chorus pertains to the subject; later poets’ choral songs that are mere interludes (Agathon’s innovation) are criticized because they might as well be transferred between plays.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acting criterion: natural sympathy and genuine feeling
rubrics_metrics.description: Those who truly feel the emotions they represent (natural sympathy or a type of creative madness) are most convincing on stage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An actor’s inner agitation or passion produces life-like reality; either natural gift or intense imaginative state allows formation of convincing character portrayals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thought: effects to be produced by speech (proof, refutation, excitation of feelings)
rubrics_metrics.description: Thought (a rhetorical category) includes every effect to be produced by speech: proof and refutation, excitation of feelings (pity, fear, anger), and the suggestion of importance or its opposite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dramatic speeches should be constructed with these aims in mind; rhetorical devices are crucial to producing intended emotional and intellectual effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incidents should ‘speak for themselves’ (treatment of incidents vs speech)
rubrics_metrics.description: Incidents must be treated so they produce their effects without separate verbal exposition; incidents should be handled like speeches when the aim is to evoke pity, fear, importance, or probability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The difference is that incidents themselves should imply the effect, whereas speeches produce the effects by what is said; avoid expository speeches that merely report what incidents already show.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diction: appropriate Modes of Expression (delivery-dependent)
rubrics_metrics.description: Diction includes Modes of Expression (command, prayer, narrative, threat, question, answer, etc.) which properly belong to art of Delivery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Knowing the mode of each utterance affects how it should be delivered and judged; some mistakes (e.g., confusing a command with a prayer) are issues of delivery rather than poetry proper.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language fundamentals and phonetics (letters, syllables, connecting words, sounds)
rubrics_metrics.description: Language comprises parts—letter, syllable, connecting word, noun, verb, inflexion/case, sentence/phrase—and attention to their phonetic and metrical properties matters for poetic composition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish vowel/semi-vowel/mute, syllable composition, aspirated vs smooth, long vs short, and the metrical consequences; inquiry into these belongs to metre and diction studies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Word types and diction choices (simple, compound, current, strange, metaphorical, ornamental)
rubrics_metrics.description: Words may be simple, double/compound, triple, etc., and classified as current, strange, metaphorical, ornamental, newly-coined, lengthened, contracted, or altered — these choices affect poetic diction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use current words appropriately for audience; be aware when a word is strange or local; employ metaphor (transference among genus/species) deliberately as part of style and meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Metaphor: types and justified transferences
rubrics_metrics.description: Metaphor involves transference of an alien name by genus-to-species, species-to-genus, species-to-species, or by analogy; it is a key figure of diction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select metaphors that reveal likeness or aptness; metaphor is a primary mode of stylistic invention and should be used to enrich expression rather than as gratuitous ornament.
